## Introduction

This note documents our Python replication of several prominent asset
pricing factor models and their extension to the international markets in the
JKP database. We thank the [WRDS team](https://wrds-www.wharton.upenn.edu/pages/wrds-research/applications/risk-factors-and-industry-benchmarks/fama-french-factors-ciz-format/),
as well as Professors [Kenneth R. French](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data_library.html), [Robert F. Stambaugh](https://fnce.wharton.upenn.edu/profile/stambaug/), and [Lin Sun](https://sites.google.com/view/linsunhome),
for providing the data and/or code that made this replication possible.

## Data & method

We assess the quality of our replication by comparing the US factors against
the published reference series. For the international panels, no official
reference data exist, so we make discretionary implementation choices that
follow the spirit of the original US methodologies. Our implementation
produces both the US and international factor return series, together with
the underlying firm characteristics.

### Factors we replicate:

- **FF3** (Fama–French 1992, 1993, 2023) — SMB is the size factor (small minus big)
  and HML is the value factor (high minus low book-to-market), both
  constructed from a 2×3 size × book-to-market sort.
- **FF5** (Fama–French 2015) — SMB is the redefined size factor (averaged
  across 2×3 size × book-to-market, profitability, and investment sorts),
  HML is the value factor, RMW is the profitability factor (robust minus
  weak), and CMA is the investment factor (conservative minus aggressive).
- **UMD** (Carhart 1997) — UMD is the momentum factor (up minus down),
  constructed from prior 12-month returns excluding the most recent month
  within size buckets.
- **HXZ** q-factors (Hou, Xue, and Zhang 2015) — ME is the size factor, IA is
  the investment factor, and ROE is the profitability factor, all
  constructed from a 2×3×3 sort on size, investment-to-assets, and return
  on equity.
- **MP** (Stambaugh and Yuan 2017) — MGMT and PERF are long–short composite
  mispricing factors constructed from 11 anomalies grouped into management
  and performance clusters, while SMB is the size factor from the
  corresponding 2×3 size-by-mispricing sorts.
- **DHS** (Daniel, Hirshleifer, and Sun 2020) — FIN is the financing factor,
  constructed from the overlap of net stock issuance and composite share
  issuance, and PEAD is the post-earnings-announcement drift factor,
  constructed from cumulative abnormal returns around quarterly earnings
  announcements. Our implementation additionally produces daily FIN and
  PEAD factors. Because the original code does not provide daily reference
  series, these daily factors are not included in the Appendix.

```{python}
#| label: setup
import sys, os
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath("."))

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import polars as pl
from IPython.display import HTML, Markdown, display
from plot_cumsum_usa import (
    MODELS,
    daily_factor_period_stats,
    date_window_note,
    factor_period_stats,
    full_sample_summary,
    load_jkp_usa,
    load_jkp_usa_daily,
    model_axis_limits,
    single_panel_figure,
)

jkp = load_jkp_usa()
jkp_daily = load_jkp_usa_daily()
specs = {m.name: m for m in MODELS}


def appendix_daily(name):
    spec = specs[name]
    for display_name, _, _ in spec.panels:
        df = daily_factor_period_stats(spec, display_name, jkp_daily)
        display(Markdown(f"**{display_name}**"))
        display(HTML(df.to_pandas().to_html(index=False)))


_model_limits = {}


def factor_tab(name, factor):
    spec = specs[name]
    if name not in _model_limits:
        _model_limits[name] = model_axis_limits(spec, jkp)
    xlim, ylim = _model_limits[name]
    fig = single_panel_figure(spec, factor, jkp, xlim=xlim, ylim=ylim)
    display(fig)
    plt.close(fig)


def section_tables(name):
    spec = specs[name]
    display(Markdown(f"*{date_window_note(spec, jkp)}*"))
    display(Markdown("*All Mean and StD figures are annualized.*"))
    display(Markdown("**Full sample**"))
    display(HTML(full_sample_summary(spec, jkp).to_pandas().to_html(index=False)))

    parts = ["<details><summary><strong>Breakdown by decade</strong></summary>"]
    for display_name, _, _ in spec.panels:
        decade_df = factor_period_stats(spec, display_name, jkp).filter(
            pl.col("Time Period") != "Full Sample"
        )
        parts.append(f"<h4>{display_name}</h4>")
        parts.append(decade_df.to_pandas().to_html(index=False))
    parts.append("</details>")
    display(HTML("\n".join(parts)))
```

### Sample windows:

- **FF3 and UMD** — July 1926 onwards. We compare against the full
  published FF3 and momentum series, which begin in July 1926.
- **FF5** — July 1963 onwards. The published FF5 series begins in July
  1963, reflecting the Compustat coverage required for the profitability
  and investment factors.
- **HXZ** — January 1972 onwards. We follow the Hou, Xue, and Zhang
  methodology and do not use the Hou et al. (2019) 1967–1972 backward
  extension. Compustat coverage in those years is thin. The US sample
  therefore starts in January 1972, as in the original paper.
- **MP** — January 1963 to December 2016. The comparison spans the
  published Stambaugh–Yuan series, which starts in January 1963 and ends
  in December 2016.
- **DHS** — July 1968 onwards (PEAD October 1971 onwards). FIN begins in
  July 1968; PEAD begins in October 1971, once quarterly
  earnings-announcement coverage is dense enough. The
  Daniel–Hirshleifer–Sun reference series end in December 2024.

These windows describe the reference series only. Our code produces the
factor return series and characteristics through the most recent available
date, even where the reference series was not extended that far.

## Reasons for divergence

- **Compustat restatements.** Compustat is updated continuously, so
  accounting variables for older fiscal years get revised over time,
  which shifts any sort that conditions on accounting data.

- **Differences in CRSP Legacy vs CRSP V2.** Historical fields
  — delisting returns, share codes, exchange codes — differ between
  the two CRSP products.

- **Unspecified implementation choices.** The published methodology may
  not fully document every construction decision, making exact
  replication require original code and data vintage.

## Conclusion

Overall, the replicated JKP factor series closely track the published
U.S. factors and are suitable for use as research substitutes. Beyond
reproducing the U.S. factors, this project extends the methodology to
the international sample, providing factors for countries where no
comparable public benchmark is available. The entire construction
process is open source and can be reproduced end-to-end from raw WRDS
data.

Note on downstream characteristics. To improve consistency with
the published factor series, we implemented several revisions to the
factor construction methodology. As a result, these changes propagate
to all factor-dependent characteristics and materially affect the
values of the factors and characteristics associated with
`mispricing_mgmt`, `mispricing_perf`, `iskew_ff3_21d`, `resff3_12_1`,
`resff3_6_1`, `ivol_ff3_21d`, `iskew_hxz4_21d`, and `ivol_hxz4_21d`
throughout the sample.

## Appendix: Replication of daily data

```{=html}
<details class="appendix-dropdown">
<summary><strong>Show daily replication tables</strong></summary>
```

Daily factor returns are mechanically noisier than monthly returns:
small differences in universe filters, delisting handling, or trading
calendars compound day-by-day, so day-level correlations are typically
lower and day-level Mean / StD figures more dispersed than at the
monthly frequency. The tables below mirror the monthly **breakdown by
decade**, with a Full Sample row at the top, computed on daily data
(Mean × 252, StD × √252).

### FF3

```{python}
appendix_daily("FF3")
```
